en: Abhidhānottaratantra, chapter 32 [Tibetan and Sanskrit, 35], Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition;
1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
Now, furthermore, I shall briefly explain the supreme secret:
one should instantly assume one's own body in the form of Śrī Heruka.
Śiva is blue, fierce, and deformed, with three eyes and six excellent faces; he bears the crescent moon in his matted hair and possesses the supreme universal vajra;
he has a crown of skull-garlands and is adorned with a garland of vajras.

With a shaven head, wearing a garland of skulls, her body fierce, and adorned with the six mudrās upon her person; clad in a tiger skin, she stands eternally with one foot placed firmly upon the body of Vārāhī.
The right face is yellow, the left is smoky-grey and red,
and the upper horse-head is white, brilliant, fierce, and terrifying;
he is embraced by the Goddess who presses against his lower body, and they are united with the vajra and bell.
Clad in a garment of tiger-skin, upholding the lineage of the Ḍākinīs,
bearing a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, adorned with the vajra-sign and other ornaments,
his hands occupied with a noose and a bell, and holding a ḍamaru drum and a severed head.
Likewise, with twelve arms, she holds a *kartṛkā* and an axe;
one should visualize all those goddesses of the mandala as having only one leg,
and likewise as having the faces of elephants, donkeys, cows, and horses.
The first has the face of a dog, the second is born from the face of an owl;
the third has the face of a boar, and the fourth has the face of a crow.
Established upon the seat, he is the embodiment of Dharma, the Great One who assumes various forms.
I am the possessor of infinite knowledge, and I am omniscient in every respect.
One should contemplate one's own state according to whatever form of body is desired;
that Great-Souled One sports in manifold forms, just like a jewel.
The thirty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Sadhana of Viśvarūpa, in the Abhidhānottarottara.

[1244'] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen traveling by sea and saw that they were in danger of being destroyed by a great yakṣa. Seeing this, he resolved to save them from their peril. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a yakṣa, went to where those five hundred merchantmen were. Having arrived there, he addressed the five hundred merchantmen, saying: "O merchantmen, do not fear; you have no cause for alarm. I am the yakṣa who will protect you from this great yakṣa. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, manifesting himself as a yakṣa, seized the great yakṣa with his left hand and held him aloft with his right hand. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having seized the great yakṣa, spoke these words to the five hundred merchantmen: "O merchantmen, do not fear; you have no cause for alarm. This is the great yakṣa who has come to destroy you. I shall now subdue him. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, manifesting himself as a yakṣa, struck the great yakṣa with his fist. Struck by the fist, the great yakṣa vomited blood and fell to the ground. Having fallen, he was unable to rise again. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having subdued the great yakṣa, released the five hundred merchantmen and restored them to safety. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, through his great compassion, rescued the five hundred merchantmen from the jaws of death. This is called the second chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s manifestation as a yakṣa.
